title: CSC3710 2026-08-25: DFAs, game FSMs, and set theory review

questions.q: Which of the following are parts of a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) under the course's definition?
choices: A finite set of states
An alphabet of input symbols
Exactly one initial (start) state
A set of final (accepting) states, possibly empty
Transitions: one outgoing arrow per alphabet symbol from every state
A tape the machine can write on
A stack for storing symbols
questions.explain: A DFA is the 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F): states, alphabet, transitions, initial state, and final states. A writable tape belongs to Turing machines. A stack is not part of a DFA.

questions.q: A DFA is allowed to have no final states at all.
questions.explain: The set of final states can be empty (F = ∅). You only have to specify which states, if any, are final.

questions.q: In a DFA, every state can be a final state.
questions.explain: The set of final states can be none, some, or all of the states.

questions.q: A DFA may have two initial states, as long as both are marked.
questions.explain: A DFA has exactly one initial state. That is the special state where processing always begins.

questions.q: What makes a finite automaton deterministic?
choices: From every state there is exactly one outgoing transition for each symbol of the alphabet
It has exactly one final state
Every state has at least one outgoing transition
No state has a transition back to itself
questions.explain: For each state and each input symbol, the next state is fixed: exactly one arrow per symbol out of every state. How many final states there are and whether there are self-loops have nothing to do with it.

questions.q: What is the alphabet of a DFA?
choices: The finite set of input symbols the machine understands
The set of states the machine can be in
The set of strings the machine accepts
The labels of the final states
questions.explain: The alphabet is what the machine understands as input. For the vending machine it is {quarter, half-dollar}.

questions.q: The vending-machine DFA from class accepts quarters and half-dollars. What is its alphabet?
choices: {quarter, half-dollar}
{accept, reject}
{insert, dispense}
questions.explain: The alphabet is the set of possible inputs, which here are the two coins. Its size is 2.

questions.q: 'Automaton' is another word for what? (one word)
questions.explain: Automaton means machine. The course uses the two words interchangeably.

questions.q: What is the plural of 'automaton'?
questions.explain: One automaton, two automata.

questions.q: How many transitions must a DFA have?
choices: (number of states) × (size of the alphabet)
(size of the alphabet)²
(number of states)²
(number of states) + (size of the alphabet)
questions.explain: Every state needs one arrow per symbol, so it's states × |Σ|. 'Inputs squared' only gives the right number when the number of states equals the alphabet size, as with 5 states and 5 inputs.

questions.q: A DFA has 6 states over an alphabet of 5 symbols. How many transitions must it have?
The vending-machine DFA has 5 states over the alphabet {quarter, half-dollar}. How many transitions does it have?
questions.explain: 5 states × 2 symbols = 10, so there are two arrows out of every state.

questions.q: A DFA has 4 states over the alphabet {0, 1, 2}. How many transitions must it have?
A DFA over the alphabet {a, b} has exactly 30 transitions. How many states does it have?
questions.explain: transitions = states × |Σ|, so states = 30 / 2 = 15.

questions.q: In JFLAP, if symbols a and b both take a state to the same target, JFLAP draws one arrow labeled with both symbols. That counts as one transition.
questions.explain: It is still two transitions, one for a and one for b. JFLAP just draws them on a single arrow.

questions.q: A machine has 3 states over {a, b} and 6 arrows in total, but one state has two arrows labeled a and none labeled b. This machine is a DFA.
questions.explain: The total of 6 = 3 × 2 is right, but the total alone doesn't prove anything. Every state needs exactly one arrow for each symbol, and this state has two for a and none for b.

questions.q: The game-programming book's monster-attitude diagram has 5 states and 5 inputs, about 11 transitions, no marked start state, and no final states. Which are valid reasons it is NOT a DFA under our course's definition?
choices: No initial state is marked
It has too few transitions: 5 states and 5 inputs need 25
It has no final states
It models a game character instead of a math problem
questions.explain: A DFA needs a marked initial state and an arrow for every input from every state (5 × 5 = 25). Having no final states is allowed (F = ∅), and what the machine models doesn't matter.

questions.q: The monster FSM has 5 attitude states and 5 possible inputs (player seen, player attacks, player gone, monster hurt, monster healed). How many transitions would it need to be a complete DFA?
questions.explain: 5 states × 5 inputs = 25. That means five arrows out of every state.

questions.q: Under our course's definition, a missing transition in a diagram can be read as 'stay in the same state'.
questions.explain: Some books and programmers assume this, but our definition requires an explicit arrow for every input from every state. If an arrow is missing, the machine is not a DFA.

questions.q: In the monster-attitude FSM, what plays the role of the DFA's alphabet?
choices: The inputs: player seen, player attacks, player gone, monster hurt, monster healed
The monster's attitudes, such as Annoyed and Mad
The AI code that runs in each state
The arrows in the diagram
questions.explain: The inputs are the alphabet. The attitudes are the states, and the arrows are the transitions.

questions.q: The monster is Uncaring and the player attacks. According to the FSM, what state does the monster move to?
choices: Mad
Annoyed
Uncaring
Rage
questions.explain: Uncaring + player attacks → Mad. (Uncaring + player seen → Annoyed.)

questions.q: When the monster is already in a top-anger state and gets hurt, it stays in the same state. How is that drawn in a state diagram?
choices: A self-loop: an arrow from the state back to itself
No arrow at all
An arrow back to the initial state
A double circle around the state
questions.explain: Staying in the same state is still a transition, so it needs an arrow. The book's diagram left this self-loop out, so it didn't match its own table.

questions.q: What is the main practical advantage of describing an NPC's behavior with a finite state machine diagram?
choices: It is a short description that can only be read one way
It runs faster than any other code
It removes the need to write any code
It lets the NPC behave randomly
questions.explain: Instead of pages of prose, a state diagram describes the behavior compactly and unambiguously.

questions.q: According to the game-programming chapter shown in class, which of these are uses of finite state machines in games?
choices: Managing the game world
Simulating an NPC's emotions
Maintaining the status of the game
Parsing input from the human player
Rendering 3D graphics
Compressing texture images
questions.explain: The chapter lists managing the game world, simulating NPC emotion, maintaining game status, and parsing player input.

questions.q: In what order does the course study machines, from least to most powerful?
choices: DFAs → nondeterministic finite automata → pushdown automata → Turing machines
Turing machines → pushdown automata → nondeterministic finite automata → DFAs
Nondeterministic finite automata → DFAs → Turing machines → pushdown automata
DFAs → Turing machines → nondeterministic finite automata → pushdown automata
questions.explain: The course starts with DFAs and builds up through more powerful machines to Turing machines. You can't start with Turing machines.

questions.q: What does a Turing machine add on top of simpler automata?
choices: A tape it can write on and move along
A second initial state
An infinite alphabet
The ability to have no final states
questions.explain: The Turing machine adds a tape that the machine can write on and move along. The idea is simple, but it is the basis for what algorithms can do.

questions.q: The ACM A.M. Turing Award, often called the 'Nobel Prize of computing', is mainly given for:
choices: Lifetime contributions to computer science
The single best paper of the year
Winning a programming contest
The most-downloaded software of the year
questions.explain: It honors contributions to the field over a career, not a single result. The prize is now $1 million, split among co-winners.

questions.q: Where does the name of the RSA cryptosystem come from?
choices: The first letters of the last names of Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman
The phrase 'Random Secure Algorithm'
The phrase 'Rapid Symmetric Assembly'
The initials of the university where it was invented
questions.explain: R, S, A are the first letters of Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman. They won the Turing Award together.

questions.q: Turing Award winner Donald Knuth created which typesetting system, the one LaTeX is built on?
choices: TeX
Markdown
PostScript
HTML
questions.explain: Knuth created TeX. LaTeX is built on top of it and is widely used for mathematical writing.

questions.q: Which of the following is a mathematical statement?
choices: Nashville is the capital of Tennessee.
Is 1 an element of {0, 1, 2}?
Write down the set {0, 1, 2}.
questions.explain: A statement is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both. Questions, commands, and bare expressions are not statements.
1 is one of the three elements, which are 0, 1, and 2.
The elements are the numbers 0, 1, and 2. The set {1} is not one of them.
The top-level elements are {∅} and {∅, {∅}}. ∅ appears inside them but is not itself a top-level element. Open only the outer backpack.
{∅} is one of the two top-level elements.
Nothing belongs to the empty set, so x ∈ ∅ is false for every x, including x = ∅.
{∅} is a backpack holding one empty backpack. Its only element is ∅.
The only element of {a} is a, not the set {a}. For this to be true, the right side would need {a} directly inside it, as in {{a}}.
The outer set's only element is the set {a}.

questions.q: ∅ and { } denote the same set.
questions.explain: Both mean the empty set, the set with nothing in it.
∅ has no elements. {∅} has one element, the empty set, like a backpack with an empty backpack inside.

questions.q: To decide whether x ∈ S, what should you check?
choices: Whether x is directly one of the top-level elements of S
Whether x appears anywhere inside S, at any depth of braces
Whether every element of x is in S
Whether S is inside x
questions.explain: Open only the outer backpack and look at what's directly inside. Checking whether every element of x is in S is the test for ⊆, not ∈.

questions.q: Which statement is true?
questions.explain: a is a top-level element. ∅ isn't listed in {a}. The only element of {a} is a. In {a, {b}}, b sits inside the inner set {b}, not at the top level.

questions.q: What is the difference between A ⊆ B and A ⊂ B, as used in this course?
choices: A ⊆ B allows A = B; A ⊂ B (proper subset) also requires A ≠ B
A ⊂ B allows A = B; A ⊆ B requires A ≠ B
They mean the same thing
A ⊆ B means A ∈ B
questions.explain: Both require every element of A to be in B. A proper subset (⊂) also cannot be equal to B.

questions.q: ℕ ⊂ ℝ (the natural numbers are a proper subset of the real numbers).
questions.explain: Every natural number is a real number, and the two sets are not equal.
The empty set is a subset of every set, including itself.
A set is never a proper subset of itself, because the two sides are equal.

questions.q: For every set S, ∅ ⊆ S.
questions.explain: ∀S, ∅ ⊆ S. The empty set has no element that could fail to be in S.

questions.q: Which of these is true?
questions.explain: ∅ is a subset of every set. It is not an element of {a}, because no empty backpack is listed. {a} is not an element of itself, and it is not a proper subset of itself.
Repetitions don't count in sets, so both sets have exactly the elements 1 and 2.
The two sets are equal, so neither is a proper subset of the other.
a is in the left set, but the right set contains {a}, not a. One counterexample is enough. ({b} is another.)
The only element of {∅} is ∅, and ∅ is not a top-level element of the right-hand set. (Note that {∅} ∈ that set is true. ∈ and ⊆ ask different questions.)
Order doesn't matter in sets.

questions.q: (a, b) = (b, a), where a ≠ b
questions.explain: Round parentheses make a sequence (here an ordered pair), and order matters in sequences.

questions.q: What is enough to show that A ⊆ B is false?
choices: One element of A that is not in B
One element of B that is not in A
Showing that A and B have different cardinalities
Showing that A ≠ B
questions.explain: A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B, so one counterexample disproves it. An element of B missing from A, or A ≠ B, only rules out A = B. A smaller A can still be a subset.

questions.q: In which kind of collection is {1, 2, 2} different from {1, 2}?
choices: A multiset
A set
Both a set and a multiset
Neither
questions.explain: Multisets count repetitions. You used them for combinations with repetition in discrete math. Sets ignore repetitions.

questions.q: A sequence of two elements, written with round parentheses so that order matters, is called a(n) ____.
questions.explain: (a, b) is an ordered pair. When a ≠ b, (a, b) ≠ (b, a).

questions.q: What is the power set 𝒫(S) of a set S?
choices: The set of all subsets of S
The set of all elements of S
The set of all proper subsets of S
The number of subsets of S
questions.explain: 𝒫(S) is the set of all subsets of S. It includes ∅ and S itself.
∅ is missing. ∅ is a subset of every set, so every power set contains it. The correct power set has 2³ = 8 elements.
All four subsets are there. Order doesn't matter: {b, a} = {a, b}, and the order in which the subsets are listed doesn't matter either.
The only subset of ∅ is ∅ itself, so the power set has exactly one element: ∅.
𝒫(∅) = {∅}, which has one element. ∅ has zero elements.

questions.q: What is 𝒫({∅})?
questions.explain: {∅} has one element, so it has 2¹ = 2 subsets: ∅ and {∅} itself.
A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, and 2⁴ = 16.

questions.q: How many elements does 𝒫({a, b, c}) have?
questions.explain: 2³ = 8: ∅, three singletons, three pairs, and {a, b, c}.

questions.q: For an arbitrary set S, which of these are always elements of 𝒫(S)?
choices: S
questions.explain: ∅ ⊆ S and S ⊆ S always hold, so both are in 𝒫(S). {∅} is in 𝒫(S) only if ∅ is an element of S. {S} is in 𝒫(S) only if S is an element of itself, which is not true in general.
The elements of a power set are subsets. Since {a} ⊆ {a, b}, {a} is an element of 𝒫({a, b}).

questions.q: What is |∅|?
questions.explain: The empty set has no elements.

questions.q: What is |{∅}|?
questions.explain: There is one item in the backpack: an empty backpack.

questions.q: What is |{ {a, b, c} }|?
questions.explain: Count only top-level elements. There is one backpack, no matter what's inside it.
There are two top-level elements: the set {1} and the set {2}.

questions.q: What is |{a, a, b}|?
questions.explain: Repetitions don't count: {a, a, b} = {a, b}.
There are three different top-level elements. Don't look inside the inner backpacks.
The intersection is {2, 3}.

questions.q: What is |{x, y} ∩ {z}|?
questions.explain: The sets have no common elements, so the intersection is ∅.
The first set contains the numbers 1 and 2. The second contains the sets {1} and {2}. They share no elements.

questions.q: Two sets that have no elements in common (their intersection is ∅) are called ____.
questions.explain: A ∩ B = ∅ means A and B are disjoint.

questions.q: What is A ∩ B?
choices: The set of elements that are in both A and B
The set of elements that are in A or B
The set of elements that are in A but not in B
The set of all pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B
questions.explain: The intersection holds the common elements, the ones where the two sets overlap.
